newsitem.title: FRANCE: New MATIF sugar contract has trades 232 on day one.
newsitem.headline: New MATIF sugar contract has trades 232 on day one.

text.p: French futures exchange MATIF notched up more than 200 trades on the first day of its new 100-ICUMSA sugar contract, the exchange reported Friday.

The new contract, announced May 23, is designed to offer hedging facilities for a lesser-quality type of sugar that better matches world trade flows than the existing contract, which is being upgraded to a 45 ICUMSA contract from October.
Icumsa (International Commission for Uniform Method of Sugar Analysis) ratings measure the colouring of sugar and are an indication of quality.
MATIF said the first month quoted, October, opened at $296/tonne on Friday before settling at $294.50 on contract volume of 130 lots.
The total market volume -- seen as active for a European commodity futures launch -- was 232 lots, compared with 590 lots on the old-style white sugar contract.
Sugars with ratings close to 100 are mainly produced in South America, Central America and Asia and currently account for over a third of world trade.
But they were only partially covered by contracts in New York, London, or Paris, MATIF said before the launch.
French officials said last week that Brazil and central America would be pivotal for the success of the new contract.
Bruno Guiot, commodities product manager at holding company Matif SA, said there was clearly demand for a 100-ICUMSA contract from the trade and major sugar producers.
"The world sugar market experienced a large move over 10 years and in the futures market nothing was done to reflect this," Guiot told a London news conference.
"The demand for this contract appeared two years ago when Brazil started to export these sugars in a massive way. Brazil and central America will play a key role," he said.
Brazil, Thailand and Guatemala have all roughly doubled their white sugar production since 1989/90.
Brazil's exports have surged by even more.
The French exchange is banking on succeeding with the new lesser-quality white sugar contract where New York's CSCE exchange failed.
Guiot said the huge activity in raw sugar futures in New York had prevented brokers there from putting resources into the development of any new contract.
The exchange acknowledges, however, that white sugar does present more technical problems than raw sugar.
Trading began in New York's white sugar futures contract, also with a maximum of 100-ICUMSA, on the CSCE last June.
But volume and open interest have been patchy.
MATIF has not given a volume target for the new contract.
But it estimates the total amount of white sugar which can theoretically be hedged against its new pit-based contract at five million tonnes a year.
That is equivalent to 100,000 lots or about 400 lots per trading day.
